query:
Sample: as-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg (no heat treatment known), mounted in phenolic, prepared by belt sanding, SiC papers P320 to P1200, 1 um alumina suspension on a napped pad (about 12 min), then 0.1 um water-based polycrystalline diamond suspension on a vibratory polisher (Buehler VibroMet 2, medium-nap synthetic cloth, 1-2 h), then ultrasonic cleaning in DI water and ethanol. No colloidal silica was used. Imaged at 5 kV in an Apreo SEM with both the Everhart-Thornley detector and a dedicated BSE detector; both detectors show the same contrast:
- angular, flat-topped particles 0.3-1.5 um across (median equivalent diameter 0.43 um), BRIGHTER than the Al matrix; about one per 26 um^2 (about 0.9% area fraction); some sit in small pockets with a dark rim;
- at 35,000x, a continuous network brighter than the cell interiors, spacing 0.5-0.8 um, all aligned in one direction across an 11.8 um field;
- dark spots 0.06-0.35 um (median 0.09 um), about 1.8 per um^2, darker than the matrix.
Questions:
(1) What are the bright particles most likely to be? Evaluate each candidate: eutectic or coarsened Si particles (including the coarse zones at melt-pool boundaries), Fe- and Mn-rich intermetallics (beta-Al5FeSi, alpha-Al(Fe,Mn)Si, pi-Al8FeMg3Si6), Mg2Si, oxides (Al2O3, MgO, MgAl2O4 spinel), embedded abrasives (alumina, SiC, diamond), and metallic debris (steel, zinc-plated steel, brass, saw-blade bond). For each, give the expected BSE contrast relative to the Al matrix and its EDS signature. Are sub-micron to micron Fe-rich intermetallic particles reported in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, at what size and number density, and do they appear bright in BSE? What Fe content is typical of LPBF AlSi10Mg powder, and does Fe partition to the cell boundaries?
(2) Is a bright cellular network in BSE consistent with the Si-rich eutectic cell boundaries of as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, and what cell size is typical? How much could polishing relief from a 1-2 h napped-cloth diamond polish contribute?
(3) Given that the dark spots are dark in BSE as well, are they more consistent with embedded 0.1 um diamond, pores or pits, Mg2Si or oxides, or organic residue? Is diamond embedding in aluminum from fine diamond suspensions documented?
(4) What EDS conditions (beam energy, spot vs area, standards) can identify 0.3-1.5 um particles in an Al matrix, given the interaction volume at 5 kV and 15 kV?
Cite primary literature and manufacturer application notes, and say clearly where evidence is missing.
task_summary: Identify And Evaluate Bright Particles Cellular BSE Network Dark Spots And EDS Conditions

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.

- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Sample: as-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg (no heat treatment known), mounted in phenolic, prepared by belt sanding, SiC papers P320 to P1200, 1 um alumina suspension on a napped pad (about 12 min), then 0.1 um water-based polycrystalline diamond suspension on a vibratory polisher (Buehler VibroMet 2, medium-nap synthetic cloth, 1-2 h), then ultrasonic cleaning in DI water and ethanol. Abstract:
Tailoring heat treatments for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) processed materials is critical to ensure superior and repeatable material properties for high-end applications. This tailoring requires in-depth understanding of the LPBF-processed material. Therefore, the current study aims at unravelling the threefold interrelationship between the process (LPBF and heat treatment), the microstructure at different scales (macro-, meso-, micro-, and nano-scale), and the macroscopic material properties of AlSi10Mg. A similar solidification trajectory applies at different length scales when comparing the solidification of AlSi10Mg, ranging from mould-casting to rapid solidification (LPBF). The similarity in solidification trajectories triggers the reason why the Brody-Flemings cellular microsegregation solidification model could predict the cellular morphology of the LPBF as-printed microstructure. Where rapid solidification occurs at a much finer scale, the LPBF microstructure exhibits a significant grain refinement and a high degree of silicon (Si) supersaturation. This study has identified the grain refinement and Si supersaturation as critical assets of the as-printed microstructure, playing a vital role in achieving superior mechanical and thermal properties during heat treatment. Next, an electrical conductivity model could accurately predict the Si solute concentration in LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg and allows understanding the microstructural evolution during heat treatment. The LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg conditions (as-built (AB), direct-aged (DA), stress-relieved (SR), preheated (PH)) show an interesting range of superior mechanical properties (tensile strength: 300–450 MPa, elongation: 4–13%) compared to the mould-cast T6 reference condition.

Abstract:
A new approach is proposed that identifies three different zones of the Si-rich network structure (the cellular structure) in laser powder bed fused (LPBF) AlSi10Mg alloy, based on the variation in morphology, grain growth transition, and melt pool solidification conditions. The three identified zones are denoted in the present work as the liquid solidification zone (LSZ), the mushy solidification zone (MSZ), and the heat affected zone (HAZ). The LSZ is the result of liquid–solid transformation, showing small planar growth at the boundary and large cellular growth in the center, while the MSZ is related to a semisolid reaction, and the HAZ arises from a short-time aging process. The boundary between the LSZ and MSZ is identified by the change of grain growth direction and the Si-rich network advancing direction. The boundary between MSZ and HAZ is identified by the start of the breakdown of the Si-rich network. In addition, it is found that the fracture is generated in and propagates along the HAZ during tensile tests.

## 1. Sample Preparation for Electron Probe Microanalysis—Pushing the Limits
Valid Text Names:
'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 1-2', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 2-5', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 5-6', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 6-9', 'geller2002samplepreparationfor pages 9-12'

BibTex:
@article{geller2002samplepreparationfor,
    author = "Geller, J.D. and Engle, P.D.",
    title = "Sample Preparation for Electron Probe Microanalysis—Pushing the Limits",
    year = "2002",
    journal = "Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology",
    volume = "107",
    pages = "627-638",
    month = "Nov",
    doi = "10.6028/jres.107.051",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.051",
    publisher = "National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "1044-677X"
}


Abstract:
There are two fundamental considerations in preparing samples for electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). The first one may seem obvious, but we often find it is overlooked. That is, the sample analyzed should be representative of the population from which it comes. The second is a direct result of the assumptions in the calculations used to convert x-ray intensity ratios, between the sample and standard, to concentrations. Samples originate from a wide range of sources. During their journey to being excited under the electron beam for the production of x rays there are many possibilities for sample alteration. Handling can contaminate samples by adding extraneous matter. In preparation, the various abrasives used in sizing the sample by sawing, grinding and polishing can embed themselves. The most accurate composition of a contaminated sample is, at best, not representative of the original sample; it is misleading. Our laboratory performs EPMA analysis on customer submitted samples and prepares over 250 different calibration standards including pure elements, compounds, alloys, glasses and minerals. This large variety of samples does not lend itself to mass production techniques, including automatic polishing. Our manual preparation techniques are designed individually for each sample. The use of automated preparation equipment does not lend itself to this environment, and is not included in this manuscript. The final step in quantitative electron probe microanalysis is the conversion of x-ray intensities ratios, known as the “k-ratios,” to composition (in mass fraction or atomic percent) and/or film thickness. Of the many assumptions made in the ZAF (where these letters stand for atomic number, absorption and fluorescence) corrections the localized geometry between the sample and electron beam, or takeoff angle, must be accurately known. Small angular errors can lead to significant errors in the final results. The sample preparation technique then becomes very important, and, under certain conditions, may even be the limiting factor in the analytical uncertainty budget. This paper considers preparing samples to get known geometries. It will not address the analysis of samples with irregular, unprepared surfaces or unknown geometries.

Abstract:
Rapid solidification techniques, such as gas atomisation, have been widely implemented in metallic alloys/composites to increase solid solubility, avoid or mitigate segregation phenomena, and favour metastable phase formation to enhance performance. Particularly, gas atomisation can enhance the solid solubility of low diffusion coefficient elements like Fe, Ni, Mn, Zr, and Cr in the α-Al matrix, yielding metastable phases. As a result, Al alloys exhibit excellent strength at high temperatures. In this study, the AISI 304L alloy was employed to introduce Fe, Ni, and Cr elements into the AlSi10Mg alloy through gas atomisation, resulting in the formation of two distinct hypereutectic AlFe-based alloys: AlFe9Si8Cr2Ni and AlFe18Si8Cr5Ni2. Gas-atomised alloy powders were separated into different size fractions by sieving and characterised using X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry, optical microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Microstructural analyses revealed dendritic patterns with distinct phases, highlighting the influence of the alloying element content on the solidification processes. Furthermore, a synergic evaluation of the XRD and EDS analysis results allowed the identification of intermetallic phases and their distribution in the two systems.

Abstract:
The present study aims to investigate the microstructural evolution and local mechanical properties of an AlFe18Si8Cr5Ni2 alloy processed via Powder Bed Fusion–Laser-Based Manufacturing (PBF-LB/M). Designed with a focus on sustainability, this alloy was produced by deriving the necessary elements from AlSi10Mg and 304L steel, two of the most widely used alloys and, consequently, among the easiest materials to source from machining scrap. By leveraging iron, chromium, and nickel from these widespread standard compositions, the alloy mitigates the detrimental effects of Fe contamination in Al-based alloys while simultaneously enhancing mechanical performance. A comprehensive investigation of the impact of rapid solidification and thermal cycling offered novel insights into phase stability, elemental distribution, and local mechanical behavior. In particular, microstructural analyses using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), field emission SEM, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and differential scanning calorimetry revealed significant phase modifications post PBF-LB/M processing, including Fe-rich acicular phase segregation at melt pool boundaries and enhanced strengthening phase formation. In addition, nanoindentation mapping was used to demonstrate the correlation between microstructural heterogeneity and local mechanical properties. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of Al-Fe-Si-Cr-Ni alloy changes after the interaction with the laser, supporting the development of high-performance, sustainable Al-based materials for PBF-LB/M applications.

Abstract:
In this work, plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) process was applied on AlSi10Mg samples, produced with laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), in the as printed condition and after different heat treatments, and, for comparison, on as-cast samples of AlSi10Mg. PEO process was performed in direct-current mode using high current densities and short time in a basic silicate electrolyte. For the first time, the effects of silicon morphology in L-PBF AlSi10Mg samples, in as printed condition and after different heat treatments, on the obtained PEO coating were investigated in terms of microstructure and corrosion properties. The microstructure of the substrate was characterized with optical and electron microscopy observations (optical microscopy OM, scanning electron microscopy SEM, and transmission electron microscopy TEM) and with X-ray diffraction (XRD). The analysis showed that heat treatments of annealing and solution treating modified the morphology and distribution of silicon in the samples obtained through L-PBF. The PEO coated samples were characterized with SEM, both on the surface and in the cross-section, and compositional analysis were performed with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis and elemental mapping. The coatings were also analyzed with XRD and the corrosion properties evaluated through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. Also microhardness tests were performed on the substrates and on the coatings. The microstructure of the coatings was strongly influenced by the silicon distribution. In particular, a non-uniform distribution of silicon and the presence of iron-rich intermetallic (obtained in the as-cast and solution treated samples) induced the formation of more porous and thinner coatings in comparison with the ones obtained in the as printed and annealed samples. The not-uniform silicon distribution produced a not-homogenous distribution of silicon into the coatings. The particular cellular structure of the as printed sample induced the formation of a coating with a higher amorphous fraction, in comparison with the ones produced on the other samples. The higher thickness and lower porosity of the coatings obtained on the annealed and as printed samples resulted in an increase of the corrosion resistance.

Abstract:
Advanced aluminides strengthened with incoherent Laves phase precipitates are promising lightweight and creep-resistant alternatives for high-alloy steels and superalloys for high-temperature critical components up to 750 °C service temperature. A significant issue with manufacturing these aluminides with conventional casting is the strong coarsening tendency of the Laves phase precipitates at elevated temperatures, leading to a significant strength reduction. In this context, the short lifetime of the melt pool in additive manufacturing and its fast solidification and cooling rates promise to consolidate these aluminides with homogeneously distributed fine Laves phase particles without coarsening. The main scientific objective of this work is to exploit the unique characteristics of the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing (AM) process to print dense and crack-free bulk Fe3Al-1.5Ta samples containing uniformly distributed (Fe, Al)2Ta Laves phase precipitates. The Fe-25Al-2Ta (at.%) alloy was selected for this work since its creep resistance at 650 °C surpasses the one of the P92 martensitic–ferritic steel (one of the most creep-resistant alloys developed for steam turbine applications). Fundamentals on process–microstructure relationships governing the L-PBF-fabricated builds are provided by a detailed microstructural characterization using X-ray diffractometer (XRD) and ultra-high-resolution scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) and high-resolution electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detectors. Orientation imaging microscopy (OIM) and grain reference orientation deviation (GROD) maps were applied to measure texture and visualize substructures within the grains. The mechanism of voids formation, morphology, and volume fraction as a function of the input energy density was identified. The melting and solidification dynamics led to microstructures with large columnar grains, porosity, and periodic cracks during the printing process. Processing samples at the building temperatures below the brittle-to-ductile transition temperature, BDTT (750 °C), often caused severe macrocracking and delamination. Crack-free samples with densities higher than 99%, some approaching 99.5%, were fabricated from pre-alloyed gas-atomized powders with a combination of high laser power (250–300 W), slow-to-medium scanning speed (500–1000 mm/s), and 800 °C build plate preheating using a 67° rotation scanning strategy. The morphology of the pores in the volume of the samples indicated a relatively sharp transition from spherical geometry for scanning speeds up to 1000 mm/s to crack-like pores for higher values. The ultra-fast cooling during the L-PBF process suppressed D03 Fe3Al-ordering. The Fe3Al-1.5Ta builds were characterized by B2 FeAl-type order clusters dispersed within a disordered A2 α-(Fe, Al) matrix. Additionally, the (Fe, Al)2Ta Laves phase (C14–P63/mmc) was predominantly formed at the matrix phase grain boundaries and frequently dispersed within the grains. The quantitative EDX analysis of the matrix gave 77.6–77.9 at.% Fe, 21.4–21.7 at.% Al, and 0.6–0.8 at.% Ta, while the composition of the Laves phase was 66.3–67.8 at.% Fe, 8.7–9.8 at.% Al, and 22.4–24.9 at.% Ta, indicating that the Laves phase is considerably enriched in Ta with respect to the matrix. The L-PBF-fabricated alloys were characterized by coarse, columnar grains which grow epitaxially from the substrate, were several m in width, and extended across several layers along the building direction. The grains exhibited a relatively strong microtexture close to <0 0 1> with respect to the building direction. The L-PBF builds showed a bulk hardness value comparable to the as-cast and spark plasma-sintered counterparts. A negligible variation of the hardness across the build height was observed. Within the framework of this study, we demonstrated that the porosity and cracking issues could be resolved mainly by controlling the process parameters and preheating the build platform above the BDTT. Nevertheless, alloy modifications and/or post-manufacturing processing are required for microstructure refinement.

Abstract:
Natural convection is present in all liquid alloys whereas forced convection may be applied as the method to improve material properties. To understand the effect of forced convection, the solidification in simple cylindrical samples was studied using a rotating magnetic field with a low cooling rate and low temperature gradient. The composition of Al–Si–Fe alloys was chosen to enable independent growth or joint growth of occurring α-Al, β-Al5FeSi, δ-AlFeSi_T4 phases and Si crystals and analysis of structure modifications. Stirring produced rosettes instead of equiaxed dendrites, which altered the secondary dendrite arm spacing and the specific surface of α-Al and also modified β-Al5FeSi. The melt flow caused a modification of iron rich δ-AlFeSi_T4 phases and gathered them inside the sample of the β/Si alloy, where δ together with Si were the first precipitating phases. The separation of δ and β phases and Si crystals was found by their joint growth along the monovariant line. A reduction in the amount of Si crystals and the formation of a thin Si-rich layer outside the sample was observed in the hypereutectic alloy. The separation and reduction in iron-rich phases may play a role in the removal of Fe from Al–Si alloys, and the control of Si may be applied in materials for the solar photovoltaic industry.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The growing use of duplex stainless steels (DSSs) has spurred extensive research and development, particularly concerning weldability challenges. The increasing interest in additive manufacturing (AM) using directed energy deposition (DED) has further highlighted the need for precise sample preparation to ensure accurate microstructural characterization. This paper consolidates best practices for preparing samples to effectively reveal microstructures and secondary phases in DSSs. By optimizing polishing techniques and etching methods, the work provides guidelines for distinguishing ferrite and austenite across the base material, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and weld metal, while also enabling the detection of intermetallic phases and discrete secondary precipitates. Examples of typical deviations, etching phenomena, and potential pitfalls are also provided. The preparation strategies presented are tailored to support subsequent analysis using light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).</jats:p>

Abstract:
The influence of chemical redissolution in the PEO layer-growth equilibrium on aluminum is evaluated differently in literature. In order to estimate whether and to what extent various alumina modifications could be affected by redissolution processes during PEO, immersion experiments were carried out on PEO coatings in model electrolytes of different alkalinity and silicate concentration. Their composition was determined spectroscopically before and after the experiments. The layers were characterized by XRD before and after the tests and examined at affected and unaffected zones using SEM, EDX, and EBSD. The results show that chemical oxide dissolution can only be observed at the layer/substrate interface and that primarily amorphous alumina is affected. This process is intensified by higher alkalinity and inhibited by silicate additives. The crystalline Al2O3 modifications show no significant attack by the electrolytes used. Transferring these observations to plasma electrolytic oxidation, they allow the conclusion that the electrochemically active zone in the pore ground of discharge channels interacts with the electrolytic and electrical process parameters throughout the entire PEO procedure. Influences of bath alkalinity and silicate content on layer growth rates are to be understood as impact on the passivation processes at the layer/substrate interface rather than chemical redissolution.

Abstract:
Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) has emerged as a powerful analytical method for the elemental mapping and depth profiling of many materials. This review offers insight into the contemporary applications of LIBS for the depth profiling of materials whose elemental composition changes either abruptly (multilayered materials) or continuously (functionally graded or corroded materials). The spectrum of materials is discussed, spanning from laboratory-synthesized model materials to real-world products including materials for fusion reactors, photovoltaic cells, ceramic and galvanic coatings, lithium batteries, historical and archaeological artifacts, and polymeric materials. The nuances of ablation conditions and the resulting crater morphologies, which are instrumental in depth-related studies, are discussed in detail. The challenges of calibration and quantitative profiling using LIBS are also addressed. Finally, the possible directions of the evolution of LIBS applications are commented on.

Abstract:
Particle-reinforced metal matrix composites (MMCs) produced using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technique have gained considerable attention because of their distinct attributes and properties in comparison with conventional manufacturing methods. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist with LPBF-fabricated MMCs: more design parameters over commercially available alloys and several defects resulting from inappropriate process conditions. These challenges arise from the intricate interaction of material- and process-related phenomena, requiring a fundamental understanding of the LPBF process to elucidate the microstructural evolution and underlying mechanisms of strengthening. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of these intricate phenomena and mechanisms, aiming to mitigate the process-related defects and facilitate the design of MMCs with enhanced mechanical properties. The material processing approach was suggested, covering from material design and LPBF to postprocessing. Furthermore, the role of in situ heat treatment on the microstructure evolution of MMCs was clarified, and several novel, potential strengthening theories were discussed for the LPBF-fabricated MMCs. The suggested strategies to address the challenges and design high-performance MMCs will offer an opportunity to develop promising LPBF-fabricated MMCs, while overcoming the material limitations of LPBF.

Abstract:
Additive Manufacturing (AM) is an advanced technology that has been primarily driven by the demand for production efficiency, minimized energy consumption, and reduced carbon footprints. This process involves layer-by-layer material deposition based on a Computer-Aided Design (CAD) model. Compared to traditional manufacturing methods, AM has enabled the development of complex and topologically functional geometries for various service parts in record time. However, there are limitations to mass production, the building rate, the build size, and the surface quality when using metal additive manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the combination of additive manufacturing with traditional techniques such as milling and casting holds the potential to provide novel manufacturing solutions, enabling mass production, improved geometrical features, enhanced accuracy, and damage repair through net-shape construction. This amalgamation is commonly referred to as hybrid manufacturing or multi-material additive manufacturing. This review paper aimed to explore the processes and complexities in hybrid materials, joining techniques, with a focus on maraging steels. The discussion is based on existing literature and focuses on three distinct joining methods: direct joining, gradient path joining, and intermediate section joining. Additionally, current challenges for the development of the ideal heat treatment for hybrid metals are discussed, and future prospects of hybrid additive manufacturing are also covered.

The excerpt does not provide the X-ray interaction-volume size or electron penetration depth specifically for aluminum at 5 kV and 15 kV, nor does it give a CASINO range result for Al. It does describe the relevant methodology: analytical resolution is governed by the convolution of the electron-probe diameter and the interaction volume, and CASINO Monte Carlo simulations are performed using the same specimen, X-ray transition, accelerating voltage, beam current, and measured probe diameter. Lowering accelerating voltage generally reduces the interaction volume and improves spatial resolution, although the reported Fe–Ni example showed measured quantitative resolution changing from approximately 800 nm at 15 kV to 200 nm at 5 kV. The text also states that high analytical resolution requires low beam currents and high accelerating voltages in the context of probe diameter, while low voltage is useful for reducing interaction-volume dimensions. Therefore, this excerpt can support the qualitative conclusion that sub-micron particle analysis generally benefits from low-voltage operation and a small probe, but it cannot determine the numerical Al interaction volumes or a definitive beam energy for EDS. Those values require a dedicated CASINO simulation or an interaction-volume calculation for aluminum.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compstruct.2020.113227, doi:10.1016/j.compstruct.2020.113227. This article has 31 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide numerical X-ray interaction-volume dimensions or electron penetration ranges for aluminum at 5 kV and 15 kV, nor does it state a specific beam energy required for analyzing sub-micron particles by EDS. It does establish that the electron-beam penetration depth can exceed the thickness of micron- and nanoscale particles, producing contributions from surrounding material and making quantitative analysis difficult. Standard bulk ZAF corrections are considered unsuitable because they assume a flat, infinitely thick specimen, assumptions that do not apply to micro- and nanoparticles. The article recommends Monte Carlo simulations, such as those implemented in SEM-EDS modeling approaches, to calculate electron trajectories, X-ray generation, absorption, fluorescence, and detector response under the actual material geometry and instrumental conditions. For determining the aluminum interaction volume at 5 and 15 kV, the relevant inputs would include aluminum composition and density, beam energy, detector geometry, and the chosen interaction-volume definition (electron range, X-ray generation volume, or analyzed volume). Selecting a beam energy for sub-micron EDS particles therefore requires matching the simulated interaction volume to the particle dimensions while limiting substrate and matrix contributions; the excerpt alone cannot identify the required numerical voltage.

The excerpt does not provide specific CASINO Monte Carlo values for the X-ray interaction volume or electron penetration depth in aluminum at 5 kV and 15 kV, nor does it state a beam energy required for EDS analysis of sub-micron particles. It explains that the analytical volume depends on the electron interaction volume, fluorescence, and the incident probe diameter; specifically, “the analytical volume is the convolution of the beam diameter with the interaction volume.” Monte Carlo simulations are used to estimate the volume and spatial resolution as a function of acceleration voltage, probe current, and detected X-ray transition. The reported FEG-EPMA probe diameters were approximately 20 nm at 5 kV and 10 pA, and 10 nm at 15 kV and 10 pA, increasing to 65 nm at 5 kV and 10 nA. The paper distinguishes quantitative resolution, observed down to about 100 nm, from qualitative resolution, observed down to several tens of nanometres. These results indicate that lower voltage and low-overvoltage conditions can reduce interaction volume and improve spatial resolution, but they do not supply the requested aluminum-specific penetration depths or an EDS beam-energy threshold.

The excerpt describes CASINO simulations for detecting nanoscale Mg2Si precipitates embedded in aluminum, but it does not provide explicit X-ray interaction-volume dimensions or electron-range penetration depths in aluminum at 5 kV and 15 kV. The reported simulations use accelerating voltages of 1 and 5 keV, with corresponding probe sizes of 10 and 5 nm. For a 5 keV beam, the text states that precipitates thicker than 20 nm can be detected using a 5 nm probe. It also reports an X-ray profile calculation for Al, Mg, and Si K lines from a 10 nm Mg2Si precipitate at 5 keV. ## pqac-00000033

From text 'martucci2025effectofpbflbm pages 6-8'.

Alessandra Martucci, Paolo Fino, and Mariangela Lombardi. Effect of pbf-lb/m processing on the microstructural evolution and local mechanical properties of novel al-fe-si-cr-ni alloy. Metals, 15:661, Jun 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met15060661, doi:10.3390/met15060661. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides relevant evidence for Fe-rich phase segregation at melt pool boundaries in a PBF-LB/M AlFe18Si8Cr5Ni2 alloy. SEM-BSE observations show coarse, bright acicular phases at melt pool boundaries, while melt pool centers contain finer, globular features. EDS mapping confirms that these coarse acicular regions are enriched in Fe. The authors attribute this recurring localization to Fe’s limited diffusivity in aluminum, associated with its larger atomic radius and poor solubility. During solidification, Fe atoms are rejected at the solidification front and accumulate in the last-to-solidify regions, identified as the melt pool boundaries. The excerpt also notes that rapid solidification can ‘freeze’ Fe diffusion and produce irregular Fe distributions. However, it does not identify the phases as pi-phase Al8FeMg3Si6 or beta-Al5FeSi, nor does it discuss AlSi10Mg in the as-built condition specifically. It also gives no nanometer-scale size measurements and does not report segregation specifically to cellular boundaries or heat-affected zones. Thus, the passage supports melt-pool-boundary Fe segregation and coarse acicular Fe-rich morphology, but not the requested phase identities, nanoscale dimensions, or HAZ/cell-boundary locations.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'martucci2025effectofpbflbm pages 8-10'.

Alessandra Martucci, Paolo Fino, and Mariangela Lombardi. Effect of pbf-lb/m processing on the microstructural evolution and local mechanical properties of novel al-fe-si-cr-ni alloy. Metals, 15:661, Jun 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met15060661, doi:10.3390/met15060661. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides relevant evidence concerning iron-rich phase segregation in a PBF-LB/M aluminum alloy, although it does not specifically study LPBF AlSi10Mg or identify the pi-phase Al8FeMg3Si6 and beta-Al5FeSi. Fe-rich, coarser acicular phases preferentially occur at melt pool boundaries, which are interpreted as last-to-solidify regions. The proposed mechanism is rejection of Fe at the solidification front, followed by accumulation at boundaries because Fe has limited diffusivity in aluminum, associated with its larger atomic radius and poor solubility. Repeated thermal exposure during layer-by-layer processing can promote coarsening of these Fe-rich phases without substantial redistribution. The excerpt also describes finer acicular and globular structures in melt pool centers, distinguishing them from the coarser boundary phases. In terms of chemistry, the boundary acicular features are enriched in Fe and depleted in Si and Al. XRD indicates that Al95Fe4Cr and Al13Fe4 remain after laser processing, with increased Al95Fe4Cr peak intensity attributed to repeated thermal cycles and enhanced Fe/Cr diffusion. The passage does not report phase dimensions in nanometers, does not mention heat-affected zones or cell-boundary segregation specifically, and does not establish the presence of Al8FeMg3Si6 or Al5FeSi.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'cattano2019feasibilitystudieson pages 143-146'.

G Cattano. Feasibility studies on laser powder bed fusion of powders mixtures based on aluminium alloys or high entropy alloys. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt does not directly identify the pi-phase Al8FeMg3Si6 or beta-Al5FeSi in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg, nor does it report their sizes in nanometers or their specific location at melt-pool boundaries or heat-affected zones. It does provide related evidence about iron-bearing phases and segregation under rapid LPBF solidification. In the studied Al-Si-Ni-Cr-Fe alloy, XRD identified a thermally stable α-Al(Fe,Cr)Si intermetallic rather than the Al13Cr2, β-AlFeSi, and Al3Ni phases predicted by Scheil calculations. The authors explain that rapid cooling can kinetically hinder formation of these predicted phases. XRD also indicated fine crystallite sizes for the α-Al(Fe,Cr)Si phase and Si. TEM showed elongated, sub-500-nm-wide α-Al cellular structures, with rejected eutectic liquid—and solutes including Si, Mg, Ni, Fe, and Cr—segregated along cell boundaries. Thus, the excerpt supports nanoscale/fine cellular segregation of Fe-containing solutes at α-Al cell boundaries, but it does not establish the requested pi- or beta-phase identity, melt-pool-boundary/HAZ location, or discrete nanometer particle size for AlSi10Mg.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'yu2016formationofintermetallic pages 21-25'.

J Yu. Formation of intermetallic phases in al-10si-0.3 fe based alloys. Unknown journal, 2016.

The excerpt provides background relevant to iron-rich intermetallic formation in rapidly solidified Al-Si-Fe alloys, although it does not specifically discuss LPBF AlSi10Mg, the pi-phase Al8FeMg3Si6, melt-pool boundaries, heat-affected zones, or Fe segregation to cell boundaries. It states that the final intermetallic population depends on Si and Fe contents together with cooling rate, and that α, β, δ, or combinations of these phases may form. Higher cooling rates promote heterogeneous nucleation and produce a higher density of smaller intermetallics, whereas lower cooling rates produce larger particles. The β-Al5FeSi phase is described as needle-like or acicular in two dimensions and as interconnected plates or blades in three dimensions; it is identified as particularly harmful to mechanical properties. The excerpt also reports that β-phase nucleation can be associated with inclusions or oxide substrates, including alumina and spinel particles, while nucleation is influenced more strongly by cooling rate than by inclusion type. For α-AlFeSi, reported morphologies include Chinese-script forms, thin sheets, bulky particles, and branched three-dimensional structures. These observations may help contextualize nanoscale or cellular intermetallic refinement under LPBF-like cooling conditions, but the excerpt does not establish the requested phase identity, precise nanometer dimensions, or preferential location at melt-pool boundaries or heat-affected zones.

## 1. qin2020rapidsolidificationand pages 1-2 (Context ID: pqac-00000040)

Rapid Solidiﬁcation and Non-equilibrium Phase
Constitution in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF)
of AlSi10Mg Alloy: Analysis of Nano-precipitates,
Eutectic Phases, and Hardness Evolution


      HONG QIN, QINGSHAN DONG, VAHID FALLAH, and MARK R. DAYMOND

         The non-equilibrium phase evolution during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of AlSi10Mg alloy
               is thoroughly characterized and analyzed by means of advanced electron microscopy and
            analytical simulation of rapid solidiﬁcation phenomenon. The evolution of microstructural
           strengthening agents such as inter-cellular eutectic phase and intra-cellular precipitates  is
           presented in correspondence with the local variation of cellular/dendritic solidiﬁcation patterns
           within a typical melt pool. The eutectic phase exhibits two diﬀerent morphologies: lamellar and
          ﬁbrous. As with the cell size variation, the overall volume fraction of eutectic phase and the
           lamella spacing is shown to gradually decrease by moving away from the melt-pool boundary
         (MPB), i.e., through crossing over from a coarse to a ﬁne cellular zone. The eutectic-free regions
           within the a-Al  cells contain a large number density of nano-sized precipitates that are
          predominantly Si-rich and are either fully or semi-coherent with the Al matrix. The formation of
           nano-precipitates is linked to the increased (non-equilibrium) solubility limits of a-Al cells due
           to the rapid solidiﬁcation eﬀect. For the ﬁrst time, we identify such nano-precipitates with
          non-equilibrium crystal structures and morphologies: ‘‘Spheres’’ and ‘‘Ellipsoids’’ with Face
          Centered Cubic (FCC), and ‘‘Plates’’ and ‘‘Needles’’ with a Diamond Cubic (DC) superlattice
           structure that emerges from within the Al matrix. The microstructure in the heat-aﬀected zone
        (HAZ) right underneath the MPB exhibits an absence of cell boundaries and eutectic phases
           while consisting primarily of large Si-rich and Mg-rich precipitates. Finally, the local variation
           of nano-hardness across a solidiﬁed melt pool is shown to correlate well with the corresponding
          proﬁle of microstructural reﬁnement, i.e., exhibiting a minimum at the HAZ and a peak at
         around the melt-pool centerline. The ﬁndings here can signiﬁcantly advance the state of
         knowledge for the strengthening behavior in an as-built LPBF-processed AlSi10Mg alloy.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion is a laser-based additive manufacturing technique that uses a high-energy laser beam to interact directly with powder feedstock. LPBF of oxide ceramics is highly desirable for aerospace, biomedical and high-tech industries. However, the LPBF of ceramics remains a challenging area to address. In this work, a new slurry-based approach for LPBF of ceramic was studied, which has some significant advantages compared to indirect selective laser sintering of ceramic powders. LPBF of Al2O3 was fabricated at different MgO loads up to 80 wt%. Several specimens on different laser powers (70 W–120 W) were printed. The addition of magnesia influenced the microstructure of the alumina ceramic significantly. The findings show that when the laser power is high and the magnesia load is low, the surface quality of the printing parts improves. It is feasible to produce slurry ceramic parts without binders through LPBF. Furthermore, the effects of SiC and MgO loads on the microstructure and surface morphology of alumina are compared and analysed.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT This article reviews advanced polishing, grinding and finishing processes for challenging manufacturing applications. The topics covered are machining of advanced alloys; machining of wafers; strengths of dies after machining; grinding and polishing for wafer level packages; hybrid finishing processes; magnetorheological finishing; cooling and lubrication; dental, implant and clinical applications; grinding of metal matrix composites; machining of other brittle materials; fixed abrasive polishing; vibratory finishing; and truing, kinematics and wear of tools. Findings include that a novel three-layered ice-bonded abrasive tool was proposed to polish Ti-6Al-4V. Wafer strengths and corresponding finishing processes are challenging issues for manufacturing of microelectronics devices. The processes could significantly enhance or reduce package strengths. Burrs were minimized to zero after grinding of honeycomb using a novel wheel with small asperities on its grinding surface. Polishing of silicon substrates using a fixed abrasive pad largely shortened the polishing time. Traditionally, grinding required flood coolant, which caused various environmental problems. Recently, more companies demand reduced coolant to respond to environmental requirements. Therefore, minimum quantity of lubrication has become a novel research trend for the benefits of the environment, health and costs. Innovative approaches led to good cooling, smooth surfaces ground with low roughness and low grinding forces. ## pqac-00000041

From text 'remond2002implicationsofpolishing pages 7-9'.

G. Rémond, C. Nockolds, M. Phillips, and C. Roques-carmes. Implications of polishing techniques in quantitative x-ray microanalysis. Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 107:639-662, Nov 2002. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.107.052, doi:10.6028/jres.107.052. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide quantitative measurements of topographic relief for different phases in aluminum alloys, nor does it directly discuss BSE contrast after diamond polishing on napped cloth. It does, however, establish that polishing relief depends on the relative hardness of adjacent phases and on the polishing substrate. Hard polishing cloths are described as producing faster removal and less relief at interfaces of different hardness than soft cloths, although they can leave a severely damaged surface. More generally, differential abrasive wear can produce a measurable step between neighboring materials: in the quartz–arsenopyrite example, the softer or more readily worn phase develops greater removal, while the harder phase remains relatively elevated. Changing to finer abrasives and final loose alumina polishing on a soft pad reduces overall roughness, but the height difference between the phases can remain visible. Thus, the excerpt supports the expectation that differential removal may generate phase relief, but it does not quantify the amount for Al alloys or demonstrate whether that relief changes BSE intensity. Any BSE-contrast effect would need separate experimental evidence, since the cited discussion characterizes surface topography using SEM, SMM, and AFM rather than correlating relief with compositional or topographic BSE contrast.

The excerpt indicates that oxide inclusions do appear in as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg. A high number density of sub-micron oxygen-rich particles is observed throughout the microstructure, particularly along cell boundaries and near eutectic lamellae or particles. The authors interpret these particles as oxide phases that were present in solid form during solidification and were pushed by the moving solid/liquid interface toward regions where final solidification occurred. The text also explains that oxidation is expected under normal LPBF chamber oxygen levels: oxide scales form at intra-track and inter-layer interfaces, are broken up by the laser during subsequent deposition, and can float in the melt pool before becoming trapped in the solidified material. The exact oxide identities are not established, but the observed oxygen-rich particles may be Si-, Mg-, and/or Al-rich, potentially including the oxide types listed in the question. This excerpt does not report their BSE imaging contrast, so it cannot establish whether they appear dark or bright relative to the aluminum matrix. info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
